paras: The burning of the Black schoolhouse at Empire, Kentucky, was an arson in early June 1881 in which 'some unknown parties' set fire to a 'negro school house' at the coal-mining settlement of Empire. No one was reported hurt and no arrests were reported, but the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian called those responsible 'scoundrels' who were 'unfit to live' and urged that they be prosecuted.

Letters from Empire describe a coal-mining settlement where the Empire Coal Co. and 'the good people of Empire' planned to build dwellings, a store, a depot and a school house. In the same issue that first noted the fire, the paper reported that Black residents of Hopkinsville were trying to bring Fred Douglass to speak on July 4th to raise money for land for a public school building.

Writing under the name QUILLER, the paper's Empire correspondent reported that 'some unknown parties burned a negro school house here last week' and that what induced anyone to set it afire was 'a mystery to the people of Empire.' Because the editor had already relayed the correspondent's report on 14 June, the fire took place before that date, and the 'last week' of the letter printed on 21 June probably refers to early June.
No report of an arrest, investigation or rebuilding of the school appears in the coverage.

Only the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian carried the story, and both of its items trace back to its Empire correspondent. On 14 June its 'Here and There' column wrote that 'the scoundrels who would do such a thing are unfit to live' and that every effort should be made to 'ferret them out and punish them to the extent of the law.' The correspondent's own letter of 21 June was flatter, placing the fire between an item on the need for a new depot and a note on a quarterly meeting at Crofton, and offering no explanation beyond calling the motive a mystery. Neither item named a suspect or the burners' race.

framing.detail: The South Kentuckian's local column called those who burned the 'negro school house' 'scoundrels' who were 'unfit to live' and urged prosecution 'to the extent of the law'.
The Empire correspondent gave the burning one line among local news and called the motive 'a mystery'.
